input:
Sampling is a critical step in the quality assessment of powder blends, because the results of any subsequent analysis can only ever be as reliable as the sample on which the analysis is performed. Unfortunately, powder blends are prone to segregation, which means that the composition of the blend may vary considerably from one part of a lot to another. This happens because particles of different sizes and densities tend to separate during handling and storage: finer particles tend to settle downwards, while coarser particles often migrate towards the top and the sides of a container, and vibration during transport can make the situation even worse.

In order to address this challenge, it is standard practice to take a series of small increments from a wide variety of locations within the lot, including different depths and, where applicable, different containers, or from across the full width of a moving stream at various points in time. These increments are then combined together to form a single composite sample, which is the sample that is ultimately analysed. The idea behind this approach is that each region of the lot should contribute to the final sample in proportion to its share of the lot as a whole.

By contrast, a single grab sample taken from one convenient location can be highly misleading. Such a sample may accurately reflect the material at the point where it was taken, but it tells us little or nothing about the rest of the lot, and it may badly misrepresent the blend's overall composition. It is also worth noting that questions of acceptance — whether the blend meets the limits set out in the site's permit — are separate from the sampling process itself, which is concerned with establishing what the blend actually contains.
target:
A powder blend is sampled to establish what the lot contains, and the sample serves that purpose only if the blend's composition can be read from it. Blends segregate. Particles differ in size and density, and handling sorts them: fines settle toward the bottom and centre of a container, coarse particles roll toward the walls and the upper layers, and vibration in transport drives the sorting further. A sample drawn from one place in the lot reports that place, not the lot.

Increments are therefore drawn from many places: across the surface and at depth, from several containers where the lot is packed in more than one, and, where the blend is moving, from the full cross-section of the stream at intervals along the run. Each increment is small. The increments are combined into one composite sample, and the composite is the sample that analysis reports. Their number and placing are set so that every region of the lot contributes to the composite in proportion to its share of the lot; an increment pattern that favours the accessible surface rebuilds the bias the pattern exists to remove.

A single grab sample misleads because it confuses a location with the lot. Taken from the top of a container, it overstates the coarse fraction; taken after transport, it reports the sorting the journey imposed. Its result is accurate for the material in the scoop and silent about everything outside it. Whether the blend passes is a separate question, judged against limits held in the site's permit: sampling establishes what the blend contains, and the permit states what it must contain.
